name: Jiaoxi Sietian Temple
address: No. 51, Sec. 1, Zhongshan Rd, Jiaoxi Township, Yilan County
description: Where other Guan Di temples enshrine a gilded statue, Jiaoxi Sietian Temple holds the only 'Silk Guan Gong' in Taiwan — an image of Guan Sheng Di Jun built up layer upon layer from silk. This is the largest and most incense-thronged Guan Di temple in northern Taiwan, dedicated to Guan Sheng Di Jun (Guan Gong) and one of the most important centers of faith in Yilan. Its graceful 'Chunqiu Tower' is a quiet delight, while the 'Turtle King' turtle-begging rite on the thirteenth day of the first lunar month is anything but quiet — worshippers borrow a fortune-turtle from Guan Di and return it, doubled, the following year. For anyone hoping to pray for career, for justice, or for peace, this is a must-visit on the way into Yilan.
history: The story begins with a monk who crossed the sea to Taiwan. In 1804, the monk Tingshuo of Zhangzhou, Fujian, carried a statue of Guan Sheng Di Jun over the water, settled in Jiaoxi, and built a temple. This was then the vital gateway for pioneers opening up the Kavalan region, and as the Han migrants of the frontier toiled to build new lives, Guan Di became the steadiest anchor in their hearts. From the Qing through the Japanese era the temple was expanded and repaired many times, and a large-scale reconstruction after the war gave it the imposing form it wears today. Branch statues of Sietian Temple's Guan Di are now found across Taiwan, its grand festivals in the first and sixth lunar months drawing great crowds — and the temple stands as one page in the history of the Lanyang Plain's settlement.

name: Penghu Tianhou Temple
address: No. 1, Zhengyi St, Magong City, Penghu County
description: Step into Penghu Tianhou Temple and the ground beneath your feet belongs to the oldest Mazu temple in Taiwan — founded before 1604 and, by documentary evidence, the very first Mazu temple on Taiwanese soil, dedicated to Mazu (the Empress of Heaven). It holds the oldest stone stele in the Taiwan-Penghu region, the tablet recording how the Ming general Shen Yourong 'ordered the withdrawal of the red-haired barbarian Weimalang' — that is, expelled the Dutch — in 1604; in 2022 the Ministry of Culture designated it a national treasure. A National Monument since 1983, the temple preserves a wealth of intact Qing-dynasty wood carving, stone carving, and painting — a living textbook for anyone wishing to see the architecture of Taiwan's earliest temples.
history: The exact founding date is lost, but a standoff at sea fixed the temple firmly in history. In 1604, the Dutch East India Company commander Wijbrand van Waerwijck arrived in Penghu with two ships; the Fujian commander Shen Yourong sailed out with fifty warships to negotiate and pressed the Dutch into withdrawing. The event was carved onto a stone stele that then slept for over three hundred years — until an 1919 renovation of the temple brought it back to light, confirming Penghu Tianhou Temple's standing as the oldest temple in the Taiwan-Penghu region. The temple was rebuilt many times through the Ming and Qing; after Shi Lang took Penghu in the Kangxi era it underwent a major renovation, and it still preserves a great deal of Qing craftsmanship today.

name: Hualien Shen An Temple
address: No. 118, Cihui 3rd St, Ji'an Township, Hualien County
description: Folk tradition holds that in the seventh lunar month of 1948, the Queen Mother of the West — Wangmu Niangniang, known affectionately as Mu Niang or Yaochi Jinmu — manifested and descended at Ji'an in Hualien; and so the Hualien Shen An Temple became the birthplace of the 'Queen Mother of the West' faith in Taiwan. Glittering and regal in style, the temple enshrines Mu Niang and holds an exalted place among the faithful. Shen An Temple and the nearby Cihui Tang share a single origin, later dividing into the Yellow-Robe and Green-Robe branches — yet as the wellspring of it all, Shen An Temple still draws countless pilgrims back to seek their roots. For anyone wishing to reach the source of Mu Niang worship, this is a stop in Hualien not to be missed.
history: Legend holds that in the seventh lunar month of 1948, the Queen Mother of the West manifested around Ji'an in Hualien and watched over the district; moved by her efficacy, the faithful built a temple to enshrine her — and this was the beginning of Shen An Temple. From here the worship of Mu Niang spread outward across Taiwan; Shen An Temple and Cihui Tang, sharing one source, branched into the Yellow-Robe and Green-Robe systems that took root island-wide. As the birthplace of the faith, Shen An Temple has been expanded many times into an ever more magnificent complex, and its annual culture festival remains a major event in Hualien — keeping generation after generation mindful of the day the Queen Mother came down to earth.

name: Hualien City God Temple
address: No. 169, Chenggong St, Hualien City, Hualien County
description: During the Japanese colonial 'kominka' campaign, many temples across Taiwan were forced to close or be torn down — the Hualien City God Temple slipped through with one clever move. The temple quietly began enshrining Koxinga (Guoxingye, whose mother, Lady Tagawa, was Japanese, so the colonial authorities regarded him as part-Japanese) and even set Koxinga's cap upon the City God, and so the temple was saved. One of the oldest temples in Hualien City, it is dedicated to the state-protecting City God (Chenghuang) and has witnessed a century of the region's change. Its architecture blends Minnan style with Japanese elements — the roof of the opera stage across the plaza still carries a distinctly Japanese flavor — and together with local snacks like the famous temple-front black tea, it anchors a lively neighborhood, a fine place to pay respects to the City God and eat well in Hualien.
history: The temple was founded in the Japanese Taisho era, around the 1920s, funded by Hualien's Han settlers as the city's foremost center of City God worship. Modest at first, it enshrined the City God attended by the civil and martial judges and the Fan and Xie generals — the well-known Seventh and Eighth Lords. As Hualien's population grew after the war, the temple was expanded several times into its present form. It has never been merely a place to burn incense: for years it has run charitable works and winter relief, a mainstay of local welfare. Its grandest moment comes with the Zhongyuan (Ghost Month) festival of the seventh lunar month, when the City God's touring procession winds mightily through the streets and draws crowds lining every road.

name: Yilan Sanqing Temple
address: No. 123, Sanqing Rd., Dongshan Township, Yilan County
description: Stand before Yilan Sanqing Temple and the whole shimmering sweep of Meihua Lake opens up before you — a rare Taoist temple in Yilan where you can offer prayers and gaze out over the water at the same time. Though the temple takes its name from its principal deities, the Three Pure Ones (Sanqing Daozu), what truly keeps the worshippers coming is Ji Gong, the 'Living Buddha,' renowned for answering prayers. Set against the mountain and beside the lake, Sanqing Temple sits in quiet, lovely surroundings — a well-known spot in Yilan for both faith and sightseeing, and just right for anyone who wants to pray to Ji Gong and unwind with a gentle wander.
history: In the 1970s, a group of worshippers chose a spot on the shore of Meihua Lake to build a temple. Legend has it that when the site was being selected, Ji Gong himself pointed to this 'dragon-vein treasure land' of superb feng shui. Sanqing Temple commands a view of the lake's waters ringed by mountains, and as word of Ji Gong's efficacy spread from mouth to mouth, worshippers came from far away. Beside the main hall to the Three Pure Ones stands a separate hall to Ji Gong. In time a full tourism belt grew up around the temple, and the Meihua Lake cycling path became a favorite Yilan destination — making Sanqing one of the few temples that balances worship and leisure so well.

name: Ji'an Qingxiu Yuan
address: No. 345-1, Zhongxing Rd, Ji'an Township, Hualien County
description: Walk into Ji'an Qingxiu Yuan and for a moment you may think you've crossed to Japan — this is the most complete Japanese-style temple still standing in Taiwan, formerly the 'Shingon-shu Yoshino Mission,' dedicated to Fudo Myoo and listed as a Hualien County historic monument. Its square 'hogyo-zukuri' pyramidal roof breathes a strong Edo-period air, and within stand the wish-granting 'Hyakudo Stone' and eighty-eight stone Buddhas modeled on the Shikoku pilgrimage circuit, lined up one by one in the deep calm of a Japanese temple. It is a lovely, quiet corner of Hualien in which to slow down.
history: In 1917, the Japanese abbot Kawabata Manji founded this mission in the Yoshino immigrant village of Hualien as a base for the Koyasan branch of the Shingon sect — and a spiritual refuge for the Japanese settlers of the day. Built in the manner of the temples of Shikoku, its hogyo-zukuri roof carries an Edo grace. After the Second World War the settlers were repatriated and the mission fell into neglect; later it was renamed Qingxiu Yuan and placed under civilian care. In 1997 it was designated a Hualien County monument, and after a thorough restoration it reopened. Its eighty-eight stone Buddhas imitate the eighty-eight sacred sites of Shikoku, so that worshippers unable to cross the ocean could make the pilgrimage close to home.

name: Taitung Tianhou Temple
address: No. 222, Sec. 1, Zhonghua Rd, Taitung City, Taitung County
description: Each Lantern Festival, the streets of Taitung stage an astonishing scene: a bare-chested strongman stands atop a palanquin and lets the crowd hurl strings of firecrackers straight at his body — this is 'Bombing Master Handan,' a folk spectacle spoken of in the same breath as 'the sky lanterns of the north and the beehive fireworks of the south.' Its stage is the Taitung Tianhou Temple, the oldest Mazu temple in Taitung, dedicated to Mazu (the Empress of Heaven), and the only official Qing-dynasty temple in all of eastern Taiwan. The temple keeps many precious plaques and relics, and its Lantern Festival 'procession of the gods' and Bombing of Handan draw tens of thousands each year, setting the faith of the 'back mountain' region ablaze.
history: The temple's origins are bound up with the putting down of a revolt. In 1889, Admiral Zhang Zhaolian, grateful to Mazu for her aid in quelling a rebellion, proposed building this temple in thanks; the Guangxu Emperor bestowed the plaque 'Numinous, Radiant, Sincere, and Protecting,' giving it the standing of an official temple from the very start. When an earthquake damaged the building in 1933, the temple was moved to its present site and repaired many times into its current form. From a Qing official temple to today's Lantern Festival spectacle, Taitung Tianhou Temple is not only a center of faith but a witness to the history of Taitung's settlement.

name: Matsu Tianhou Temple
address: No. 4, Matsu Village, Nangan Township, Lienchiang County
description: Of every Mazu temple in the world, only this one has — just a few steps before the shrine in the main hall — the 'spirit cave' where Mazu's own body is said to lie. Matsu Tianhou Temple stands beside Matsu Harbor in Nangan, facing the open sea, the single most important center of faith in the Matsu Islands, dedicated to Mazu (the Empress of Heaven). Legend tells that when Mazu's father and brother failed to return from a fishing voyage, Lin Moniang threw herself into the sea to save her father and drowned; her body drifted to the Magang inlet of Nangan, and the villagers, moved by her filial love, buried her there and raised a temple over the spot. Even the name of the Matsu archipelago comes from 'Mazu' — as early as 1894 a British naval chart marked this island as 'Matsu,' the earliest documentary appearance of the name. The annual 'Mazu Ascension Festival' on the ninth day of the ninth lunar month is the grandest religious celebration in Matsu.
history: The exact founding date is lost, but the story of this land runs very deep. People were living around the Matsu inlet of Nangan as far back as the Song dynasty — Song-era ceramic shards have been unearthed here — and the old gazetteer 'Sanshan Zhi' called Nangan 'Shanggantang,' a name changed to Nangantang only in Ming and Qing times. The temple has been rebuilt many times; among the documented records are Zhang Yizhou's 1943 'Account of the Rebuilding of the Matsu Island Tianhou Temple' and an inscription by General Peng Qichao in 1963. In 2001 the old temple was pulled down and rebuilt, with designers from the Puxian region brought in to raise a palace-style temple modeled on the Meizhou Mazu ancestral temple — the grand form it holds today.

name: Kinmen Wudao City God Temple
address: No. 40, Guangqian Rd, Jincheng Township, Kinmen County
description: Every year on the twelfth day of the fourth lunar month, the whole island of Kinmen erupts in a grand island-wide parade — art-floats and performance troupes stretching endlessly down the roads. This is the 'Kinmen City God Welcoming,' ranked among 'Taiwan's Hundred Religious Sceneries.' Its star is the Wudao City God Temple, the largest and most incense-thronged temple in Kinmen, dedicated to the City God (Chenghuang) and the island's most important center of faith. Built in a three-bay, two-hall layout beneath an imposing hip-and-gable double-eaved roof, the temple carries a long memory: the day's revelry commemorates the year 1680, when the Kinmen garrison commander Chen Long moved the administrative seat from Kinmen City to Houpu — and the City God moved with him, an incense fire now more than three hundred years old.
history: The temple's origins reach back to 1387, when Zhou Dexing, Marquis of Jiangxia, built the walled garrison at Kinmen City and raised the Gudi City God Temple alongside it. In 1663 the Qing coastal-evacuation policy left the existing City God temple at Houpu in ruins. Not until 1680 did Chen Long, the first Kinmen garrison commander, move the administrative seat to Houpu and branch the Gudi City God to the Ximen ward there — laying the foundation of the Wudao City God Temple. In 1811, Wen Yingju and others raised over 2,300 taels of silver to rebuild it, and a further expansion in 1994 brought it to its present scale. Through all this migration and rebuilding, the bond between the City God and the town of Houpu has endured for more than three hundred years.

name: Hualien Gang Tian Temple
address: No. 15, Ln. 500, Sec. 1, Zhongshan Rd, Hualien City, Hualien County
description: Hualien Gang Tian Temple is the largest Mazu temple in eastern Taiwan, dedicated to the goddess whom locals affectionately call 'Gang Tian Ma' (Mazu, the Empress of Heaven), and an important center of faith for Hualien City. Its grounds are vast and its presence commanding, its architecture blending southern and northern styles in ornate detail — the enormous archway (pailou) and the wide temple plaza make an immediate impression. When Mazu's birthday comes around, the temple holds a grand celebratory procession that gathers up all the warmth of Hualien's people — a place not to be missed when you come to worship Mazu in Hualien.
history: The temple's story begins with a golden Mazu statue that crossed the sea with migrants. In the Guangxu era, around the 1890s, early Han settlers carried a branch statue of Mazu to Hualien Port — then known as 'Qilai' — where at first they could only enshrine this earliest 'Great Mazu' in a rough thatched hut. As the incense grew through the Japanese era, the hut was rebuilt as a small wooden temple. By 1977 the old temple had grown too small, and a new one was begun on the present site in Hualien City, taking years to reach the imposing form it holds today. Its Mazu-birthday procession, held around the third lunar month, is now the grandest religious event in Hualien City each year.

name: Tafalong Ancestral Shrine
address: Tafalong Tribe, Guangfu Township, Hualien County
description: In Guangfu, Hualien, lives Tafalong — an Amis (Pangcah) settlement more than 1,500 years old, one of the oldest and largest Amis communities in Taiwan. At its heart stands the ancestral shrine (kakita'an), the core of Tafalong's spiritual life and cultural transmission. Within it are kept ceremonial vessels and the symbols of the ancestral spirits, handed down through the generations, while the shrine's pillars are carved with exquisite wooden motifs recounting the Amis creation myths and the stories of the ancestors — a precious treasure of Taiwan's indigenous art. The grandest event of the year is the Harvest Festival (Ilisin) held in July and August, when the whole community gathers to sing and dance, offering their respect to the kawas (ancestral spirits) and giving thanks for the protection of the people and the gifts of the natural world. The festival's songs and dances, its shared feasting, and its rigorous age-grade system reveal the full depth of Amis social structure and culture.
history: Tafalong's history reaches back more than 1,500 years — after the ancestors of the Amis migrated into the East Rift Valley, this was among the earliest large settlements they founded. In the Amis language 'Tafalong' means 'white crab,' a name said to come from the white crabs once abundant in the local streams. The ancestral shrine (kakita'an) is the spiritual core of the community, and in both its form and its rituals it preserves the most ancient of Amis traditions. During the Japanese colonial era, Japanese scholars carried out detailed ethnological surveys here, leaving behind valuable records. In recent years the people of Tafalong have thrown themselves into cultural revitalization — restoring the shrine, singing the old songs anew, reviving traditional crafts, and developing the 'Tafalong Cultural Park' — turning this ancient settlement into a model of indigenous cultural preservation in Taiwan.
